episode_thesis: Katy Kaminski (AlphaSimplex) and Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (Systematic Investor Ep. 356, recorded in early-to-mid July 2025, uploaded 17 July) argue that managed-futures drawdowns come when equities do well and recover quickly when equities are stressed, so trend is useful in both states, that trend should not be timed but rebalanced into (it mean-reverts at long horizons), and that trend remains one of the few robust equity complements that pays in distress. Fast-reversing exogenous shocks such as Liberation Day are the worst for trend while fundamentals-based endogenous shocks (monetary policy, inflation) tend to help. Kaminski reviews a non-parametric regime method (Harvey et al.) as an empirical filter and explains that CTA replicators outperformed in 2025 mainly because they are smaller in market set and slower, not through luck.

speakers.name: Katy Kaminski
speakers.role: Guest; trend-following researcher and chief research strategist at AlphaSimplex (Boston); lead author of the managed-futures drawdown paper discussed
speakers.speaker_note: Ledger spelling 'Katy Kaminski' (captions 'Katie Kaminsky'). Her China-markets explanation is explicitly 'my first guess'. She did not claim to have memorised replication tracking-error numbers. Remarks on the Harvey et al. regime paper are a reading of someone else's work, with her own criticisms.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend drawdowns tend to occur while equities do very well, and recoveries are faster when equities are stressed and slower when equities keep making new highs, so trend looks good coming out of a drawdown in either state.
worldview_premises.support: Her paper plotting drawdown depth, duration and recovery of the SG Trend Index against equity returns; the largest managed-futures drawdown above 10% was 2015-2019.

worldview_premises.premise: Drawdown and recovery times vary a lot, so the current drawdown could recover quickly or slowly; the CTA winter (2010-2014, second longest) came after the GFC recovery and ended with the 2014 energy collapse.
worldview_premises.support: Historical drawdown plot.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend should not be timed ('trend following squared'); because the strategy mean-reverts over longer horizons, investors should rebalance (buy after drawdowns, trim after gains), as many institutions do after a big year like 2022.
worldview_premises.support: Long histories showing 15-20% drawdowns followed by strong recoveries; institutional behaviour she observes.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following is one of the few robust equity complements that pays in distress and no better alternative has been found; institutions layer defensive diversifiers ('first, second, third responders') with trend as one layer.
worldview_premises.support: Empirical evidence including her drawdown paper and CFM work on skew; she notes papers exist with significant p-values but few with comparable robustness.

worldview_premises.premise: Fixed-income trend depends on regime: strong in falling rates with a steep curve, strong short when the curve is inverted, mixed when flat; fixed income was choppy in 2025 so trend signals gave it little weight.
worldview_premises.support: Her earlier fixed-income paper; 2025 steepening/flattening and Fed back-and-forth.

worldview_premises.premise: Initial rhetoric-driven shocks are bad for trend; trends emerge once fundamental data show the new direction (e.g., a copper tariff linked to copper). Isolated tariff events can start trends in metals; the commodity sector gives diversification most investors do not hold directly.
worldview_premises.support: Observation of copper/platinum signals building on trade tension.

worldview_premises.premise: Trump 1.0 tweets produced little trend, whereas Trump 2.0 coincides with larger global change in geopolitics, supply chains and alliances; the 2015-2019 drawdown was not mainly a trade-war effect but also reflected the very low rate environment.
worldview_premises.support: Her earlier study of Trump's tweets found little trend.

worldview_premises.premise: Exogenous shocks that reverse quickly (whipsaw) are the worst for trend but those that extend can help; Covid was less damaging than Liberation Day because supply-chain trouble was anticipated and bonds rallied, giving trends outside equities. After Liberation Day, further shocks (copper tariffs) get smaller reactions, and endogenous shocks (monetary policy, inflation), being fundamental valuation shifts, tend to help trend and are more likely next.
worldview_premises.support: Comparison of Covid and Liberation Day; turbulence metrics (magnitude-of-surprise) to size shocks.

worldview_premises.premise: A three-day shock followed by a rebound is too short to detect statistically, unlike Covid which lasted a month or two, so shorter-term trend did well in Covid but not on Liberation Day.
worldview_premises.support: Horizon argument; no data cited.

worldview_premises.premise: Pre-defining regimes (rising or falling rates) creates bias and rule-based regime definitions overfit history, so non-parametric methods and walk-forward testing that account for how many variables were tried are preferable; the Harvey et al. method uses seven standardised state variables and a Euclidean distance of the current month to all past months, then assumes strategies that did well in similar months will do well next.
worldview_premises.support: Her reading of the paper; critics say the seven variables were chosen with hindsight; she calls it data filtering and not macro.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend likely connects to recessionary regimes (e.g., an inverted curve in fixed income), which the non-parametric method could test.
worldview_premises.support: Her fixed-income paper; her stated homework assignment.

worldview_premises.premise: Replicators outperformed in 2025 mainly because they are smaller in market set and slower, so they reacted less to Liberation Day; tracking error is within the expected range; regression-based replication is the slowest, mechanical or hybrid replication faster; differences reflect market regimes (e.g., cocoa missed) not luck.
worldview_premises.support: Her replication paper's methodology (not updated since); she did not recall exact tracking-error figures.

worldview_premises.premise: Tracking error depends on market set and implementation, so investors must understand the replicator's inputs and trading to measure it; replication can be a separate strategy combined with CTAs to reduce dispersion.
worldview_premises.support: Her replication paper; client feedback.

worldview_premises.premise: China-focused CTA programs did worse than traditional CTAs in June 2025, probably because Chinese futures are commodity heavy: energies spiked and reversed on geopolitics while supply-chain metals trended differently from other markets (her stated first guess, unchecked).
worldview_premises.support: Guess; she had not looked at the data.

worldview_premises.premise: Discretionary investors who cut equities in April find it psychologically hard to buy back at record highs, whereas systematic managers are indifferent; sentiment shifted in early July 2025 toward better growth with rotation into US small caps.
worldview_premises.support: Observation of investor sentiment over the previous two weeks.

steps.from: Endogenous shocks (monetary policy, inflation, structural rates change as in 2022)
steps.to: Trends that extend, because they are fundamental revaluations
steps.why: They shift how assets are valued.

mechanism_chains.fails_when: Exogenous shocks that extend can help; in Trump 2.0 the supply-chain and alliance change may be large enough to produce sustained trends.

decision_process.practice: Do not time trend; rebalance into it after drawdowns and trim after gains.
decision_process.why: Mean reversion at long horizons; large recoveries once they begin.

decision_process.practice: Build layered defensive portfolios of different diversifiers, with trend as one layer.
decision_process.why: Trend is robust but not a silver bullet.

decision_process.practice: In 2025 fixed income was underweighted by trend signals because of choppy steepening/flattening; weight depends on regime (falling rates with steep curve, or short with inverted curve).
Use walk-forward tests and account for how many variables were tried; avoid rule-based regime definitions; prefer non-parametric similarity filters.
Use turbulence (magnitude-of-surprise) metrics to identify and size exogenous shocks when studying their effects on trend.
Evaluate replication by understanding inputs (market set, trading speed) so tracking error can be measured; treat replication as a separate strategy to combine with CTAs.
Look for fundamental data confirming the new direction rather than trading rhetoric-driven shocks.
decision_process.why: Rhetoric shocks are often bad for trend.

speakers.evidence_style: Empirical and visual (bubble charts of drawdowns against equity returns), long-history studies and her own papers; skeptical of rule-based regimes; admits what she has not checked (China markets, replication numbers).

current_views.view: Equities and a weak dollar trended most in 2025 (the dollar began to revert in July); fixed income choppy; energies spiked, reversed and rebounded in June-July; metals tied to trade policy more interesting.

Sentiment toward equities has tentatively turned positive (growth better than thought; rotation to US small caps), and systematic managers are indifferent while discretionary investors struggle to buy back at record highs.
The current managed-futures drawdown could recover fast or slowly, but is not a reason to leave; rebalance into it.
Further tariff shocks (copper) bring smaller reactions; endogenous shocks (monetary policy, inflation) are more likely next and would help trend.
Metals (copper, platinum) are building long signals on trade tension and potential tariffs, with small positioning so far.
current_views.reasoning: Isolated event linked to trend; fundamental data needed to confirm.

speakers.name: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
speakers.role: Host of Top Traders Unplugged; veteran CTA manager (35 years in the industry)
speakers.speaker_note: Reports CTA index levels and relays papers (Man Group, Ilmanen/AQR, CFM, Harvey et al.). He attributes the China-markets explanation to himself in the original ledger entry; correction: he only reported the underperformance and said he does not know why (the explanation is Kaminski's guess).

worldview_premises.premise: Trend should be judged by its portfolio effect, not stand-alone Sharpe, and it is fantastic that something typically does poorly when equities do great: it would be worse if it always did poorly when equities were poor.
worldview_premises.support: Common-sense argument; criticism of those who use Sharpe for single line items.

worldview_premises.premise: A blend of trend following and the S&P 500 gives nearly the sum of both returns, which explains the stream of new portable-alpha overlay products.
worldview_premises.support: His own return illustrations.

worldview_premises.premise: Bonds have more inbuilt momentum while equities revert (V-shapes), so fixed income gives the best trend profits.
worldview_premises.support: Ilmanen's paper (AQR) and his own return distributions.

worldview_premises.premise: The worst trend drawdown-recovery combinations coincided with Trump trade-war periods (2018 and 2025); the post-Liberation Day S&P recovery (57 days, no Fed support) was the fastest ever from a 20% drawdown, a V-shape trend following is not built for.
worldview_premises.support: Kaminski's chart and a colleague's statistic.

worldview_premises.premise: Tariff-driven positions such as long copper are fragile because the next statement can reverse them; recoveries often follow a real narrative change across a broad range of markets (e.g., rates rising after the post-GFC period).
worldview_premises.support: Examples from the CTA winter and 2022.

worldview_premises.premise: CTA index drawdowns of about 20% are small next to a 55% S&P 500 drawdown, and rolling 12-month CTA returns below -5% are rare compared to those above +15% (about 2-4 versus 59 instances, per the Man paper).
worldview_premises.support: Man paper statistic (as of end of April).

worldview_premises.premise: Investors chase performance and rarely rebalance into trend after poor returns; he sees people selling trend after it has done well.
worldview_premises.support: 35 years of industry experience.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend works because everyone gets news at the same time but digests it at different speeds: a tariff is understood instantly, Covid took time, leaving room to position short energy. CFM's work separates exogenous (Liberation Day) from endogenous (2022 rates positioning) shocks.
worldview_premises.support: CFM paper and Covid example.

worldview_premises.premise: Short-term CTAs beat long-term in April 2025 (as expected for an exogenous shock) but the order reversed in May-June.
worldview_premises.support: Official performance numbers.

worldview_premises.premise: Replicators outperforming their benchmarks in 2025 implies either a large tracking error or a separate alpha strategy rather than replication.
worldview_premises.support: Logical argument; Andrew (a replication manager) scheduled as a guest.

worldview_premises.premise: China-focused CTA programs did worse than traditional CTAs in June 2025; he does not know why (his firm does not trade Chinese markets). Staying outside the euro has served Denmark well.
worldview_premises.support: Observed programme returns; personal view on the euro.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The drawdown-state finding (drawdowns while equities do well, quick recoveries in stress) rests on equity returns as the only state variable and a graph described verbally; the causal story that trend underperforms when things are good is not tested for confounding (e.g., rates regime).

Kaminski says 'do not time, rebalance', but also says recoveries are strong once they start and the big question is when; the practical difference between rebalancing into a drawdown and timing a recovery is not defined.

Replicator outperformance is attributed to slowness and smaller market sets, but she did not recall tracking-error numbers and the paper has not been updated; the host raises luck and her response is regime variation, not a quantitative test.

The Harvey et al. regime method is described from memory with open implementation questions (how many state variables were tried, hindsight selection of seven); Kaminski's own expectation of a trend link to recessionary regimes is a hypothesis awaiting test.

The claim that Covid was less damaging than Liberation Day because supply chain trouble was anticipated and bonds rallied is an interpretation; the statement that further shocks get smaller reactions and endogenous shocks are 'more likely next' is a forecast without evidence.
The explanation for the China-focused CTA underperformance is a first guess by Kaminski, and the host's ledger attribution had to be corrected; no data was looked at.
Man paper statistics (number of rolling 12-month returns below -5% versus above +15%) are quoted from memory with an end-of-April cutoff; the exact counts (2 versus 59) are approximate.
Claim that no better alternative to trend has been found is limited to her knowledge of papers; she acknowledges papers with significant p-values exist but with less robustness.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Inputs the speakers treat as informative for trend: the equity state (drawdowns coincide with strong equities; recoveries are faster in stress), the yield-curve shape for fixed-income trend (steep with falling rates, inverted for short trend), whether shocks are exogenous and quickly reversing or endogenous (monetary policy, inflation), fundamental confirmation of tariff or trade changes in metals and other commodities, turbulence (magnitude-of-surprise) metrics, and the seven-variable similarity filter. Horizon is months for regime and drawdown recovery, but Kaminski explicitly says timing trend is not advisable; the actionable input is rebalancing.
reader_inferences: (reader) Kaminski's through-line is that trend's value is conditional and portfolio-level: it pays when equity investors most need it (distress), and its drawdowns coincide with periods when the investor's equities are doing well, so the net portfolio experience is acceptable.

(reader) Both speakers explain 2025 by shock type (rhetoric-driven exogenous shocks that reverse hurt; fundamental endogenous shifts help), which is a regime reading without a tested rule to trade on.

(reader) The replication discussion shows a general principle in the episode: the speed and breadth of a strategy's implementation matter more than its labelled category when explaining a year's relative performance.

(reader) The host's role is to supply counter-evidence and practical observation (investors do not rebalance; tariff positions fragile), and Kaminski's role is to supply conditional empirical structure.
